node.label: bell hooks
node.date_label: Ain’t I a Woman 1981 · Feminist Theory 1984 · Yearning 1990 · Black Looks 1992 · Teaching to Transgress 1994
node.description: In Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism (1981), bell hooks argued that feminism must confront racism and sexism together to understand Black women’s historical devaluation. Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center (1984) challenged the treatment of privileged white women’s experience as universal, connecting racial hierarchy with class relations. “Postmodern Blackness” (1990) criticized postmodern theory’s exclusion of Black voices while using its critique of essentialism to affirm multiple Black identities. In Talia Bettcher’s account of the exchange, Judith Butler’s Bodies That Matter (1993) challenged hooks’s reading of Paris Is Burning by emphasizing performance’s capacity both to repeat and to unsettle dominant norms.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism (1981); Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center (1984); “Choosing the Margin as a Space of Radical Openness” (1989; reprinted in Yearning, 1990); Yearning: Race, Gender, and Cultural Politics (1990); “Postmodern Blackness” (1990); “Theory as Liberatory Practice” (1991); Black Looks: Race and Representation (1992); Teaching to Transgress: Education as the Practice of Freedom (1994).
node.scope_note: Read the incomplete licensed opening-chapter preview of Feminist Theory, the complete “Oppositional Gaze” chapter and “Postmodern Blackness” essay, and selected passages of “Choosing the Margin” and “Theory as Liberatory Practice.” Higginbotham’s selected 1992 pages were freshly read. Butler’s criticism is mediated through Bettcher; both original Paris essays remain unread. Other books, translations and cited theoretical originals were not read in full.

people_update.label: bell hooks
people_update.identity_note: hooks spoke of herself as a Black person from the hills of Kentucky.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Talia Bettcher explains, Butler’s Bodies That Matter (1993) responds to hooks’s “Is Paris Burning?” (1992) by stressing that performance can reproduce and subvert dominant norms together.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Bettcher, section 5.2, paragraphs beginning “Butler also allows,” “Butler’s discussion,” and “Butler, by contrast”; adjacent 5.3 retains criticism of Butler. Mediated reading only: both original Paris essays unread. No claim that Butler considers every drag performance subversive.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center (1984), hooks challenges feminist accounts, beginning with Friedan's, that treat the situation of college-educated, middle- and upper-class white women as universal and assume a common oppression of all women.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Licensed chapter-1 preview, opening Friedan discussion and paragraph beginning “A central tenet”; no stable pagination. “Common oppression” is contested; full book unread. Adjacent theory challenges historical generalization.

proposed_edges.relationship: Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center (1984) connects racial hierarchy and capitalist class relations in explaining differences among women.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chapter-1 preview, paragraphs beginning “Yet class structure” and “White women who dominate”; selected primary argument, not authorship of Crenshaw’s later term or full-book reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Postmodern Blackness” (1990), hooks challenges postmodern theory’s exclusion of Black women while retaining antiessentialism as a resource for resistance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete official journal essay read; paragraphs beginning “As a discursive practice,” “The failure to recognize,” “Criticisms of directions,” and “Employing a critique.” “Multiple black identities” preserves her positive use of antiessentialism. This is a bounded theory intervention, not rejection of all poststructuralism or participation in a historians’ truth debate.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Feminist Killjoys (And Other Willful Subjects)” (2010), Sara Ahmed draws on hooks’s Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center (1984) for her account of the angry Black woman as a figure who is felt to kill feminist joy.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Ahmed’s complete essay on the journal’s own site (S&F Online 8.3, Summer 2010, Barnard Center for Research on Women), print version; the passage is on page 4 of 8 of the paged version, section “Feminist Tables”, paragraphs beginning “After all, feminist spaces are emotional spaces” and “It is not just that feelings are ‘in tension’”, notes 10–11. Ahmed places the feminist killjoy beside “the figure of the angry Black woman, explored so well by Black feminist writers such as Audre Lorde and bell hooks”, quotes hooks’s description of a meeting where “the atmosphere will noticeably change when a woman of color enters the room” (n. 11: hooks, p. 56, citing the 2000 Pluto edition of Feminist Theory) and builds her analysis of affective tension on it. The body text engages hooks’s account; it is not a citation-only note. Lorde is named alongside; no claim that hooks is Ahmed’s only resource. hooks’s book not reread here for this edge.

proposed_edges.relationship: hooks and Hall co-authored Uncut Funk: A Contemplative Dialogue (2018), a book of conversations begun in 1996 on conversation and writing, feminism and Marxism, home and kinship, and the costs of Black intellectual life in the academy; in a 2024 review, Tzarina T. Prater reports that hooks’s preface calls Hall “the closer kin”.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read in full Tzarina T. Prater’s review “Conversations between the Closer Kin” (SX Salon, Small Axe, February 2024), the journal’s own open review page. Its bibliographic head gives “bell hooks and Stuart Hall, Uncut Funk: A Contemplative Dialogue (London: Routledge, 2018)”. The paragraph beginning “When I started reading Uncut Funk” dates the conversations to 1996 and names Paul Gilroy’s foreword. Paragraphs beginning “They begin their discourse” and “Their ‘conversation’ is wide ranging” describe the exchange, with page references to the book. The paragraph beginning “Despite her confession in her short preface” reports that hooks identifies Hall as “the closer kin”. The reviewer also notes asymmetries (“hooks functions more as interviewer than dialogue partner” at moments). The book itself is unread: claims of content are limited to the review. This is a co-authored substantive work (contribution, undirected), not an influence claim. It does not restore held bh_w_02 (Hall’s representation argument in “The Oppositional Gaze”), which remains unread on a permitted route.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Subjects of Empire? Indigenous Peoples and the ‘Politics of Recognition’ in Canada (2009), Glen Sean Coulthard draws on hooks’s Yearning: Race, Gender and Cultural Politics (1990) to articulate a politics of self-recognition directed away from dependence on recognition by the settler state.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Coulthard’s conclusion on pp. 71–72 and note 129 in his university-deposited dissertation. He incorporates hooks’s argument into his own proposed alternative to state-centred recognition. Yearning itself was not read; the claim concerns Coulthard’s explicit use. Scholarly argument only; no community knowledge is reproduced.
